messages.subject: another rstanarm bug, this time with k-fold cross-validation, kfold()
parts:
So. I wanted to crate a model where loo would fail. I did so using fake-data simulation, creating 5 random predictors that were correlated 0.8 with each other:

library("rstanarm")
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
library("arm")
library("MASS") # needed for mvrnorm()

n <- 200
k <- 5
rho <- 0.8
Sigma <- rho*array(1, c(k,k)) + (1-rho)*diag(k)
X <- mvrnorm(n, rep(0,k), Sigma)
b <- -2 + (1:k)
sigma <- 2
z <- rlogis(n, X %*% b, 1)
y <- ifelse(z>0, 1, 0)

## First I fit the full model:
fit_1 <- stan_glm(y ~ X, family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
loo_1 <- loo(fit_1)
## I got this warning:

Warning message:
Found 23 observations with a pareto_k > 0.7. With this many problematic observations we recommend calling 'kfold' with argument 'K=10' to perform 10-fold cross-validation rather than LOO.

## OK, fine. So I do 10-fold cross-validation:
kfold_1 <- kfold(fit_1, K=10)
print(kfold_1)
## And this works just fine.

## Now I want to compare to a model removing predictor 1
Z <- X[,2:5]
fit_2 <- stan_glm(y ~ Z, family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
kfold_2 <- kfold(fit_2, K=10)
print(kfold_2)
## This works fine too.

## Then I try putting X[,2:5] right into the model (instead of giving it the new name Z):
fit_2 <- stan_glm(y ~ X[,2:5], family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
## This works fine.
## But then I try the next step:
kfold_2 <- kfold(fit_2, K=10)
## And I get an error message:

Fitting model 1 out of 10
Error in X[, 2:5] : incorrect number of dimensions

## Whassup?? The model fit fine. So why the problem with kfold()?

A

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: another rstanarm bug, this time with k-fold cross-validation, kfold()
parts: So... kfold attempts to account for the fact that sometimes data is specified using the data argument to stan_glm and other times using the global environment. When no data argument is specified it needs to construct a data frame that it can use to refit the model K times (each time modifying that data frame to drop the right set of observation). So it constructs a data frame consisting of the 2nd through 5th columns of X because that's what you implicitly told it was your data. But now when we need to go refit the model how is the formula including X[, 2:5] supposed to be interpreted relative to this data frame? There are ways around this but so far they seem to introduce other complications that are even more annoying.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: another rstanarm bug, this time with k-fold cross-validation, kfold()
parts: Also, it's really really really hard to write functions like kfold that handle all possible things a user can do when specifying a model. This is the curse of R's flexibility. It's nice to be able to write the same model in many ways but that also means it's a nightmare to make sure all of those specifications are compatible with every thing you might want to do after the fact. It would be much easier if we allowed fewer ways of specifying the same model.

On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 4:06:31 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
I'm only including code that runs! 

But, that's right, I don't want to include crap like "data=data" in all of my stan and stan_glm calls. 
A

Well, not "data=data" but maybe "data=wells" isn't so bad? Unlike the list you need to (or needed to) manually create for rstan, for rstanarm it would just be the name of the data frame where the variables in the formula can be found. I understand the appeal of not needing to do that, but I think that's outweighed by the mess it causes for software development. Here's a pros/cons list:

Cons of searching for data in global (or local) environment if not specified:

1) Takes developers a lot more time to add anything new to rstanarm because it's not easy to ensure that the data is handled appropriately. This is not an exaggeration: at most 1/4 of the time I spent implementing kfold was getting the algorithm right and the rest was spent on avoiding errors when people specify data without a data argument. And even after all that time there are apparently still cases when it doesn't work!) 
2) Inevitably more bugs because the internal code needs to be much more complicated and is harder to test
3) Easier for the user to make mistakes (need to be very vigilant about what's already in the global environment) 
4) I could probably come up with a bunch more!

Pros of searching for data in global (or local) environment if not specified:

1) A little bit less typing for the user
 
Am I missing any other advantages other than a bit less typing? I really don't want to sacrifice the quality of the software just to avoid typing something like data=wells, but if there are other advantages I'm missing then maybe those will tip the scale. 

Jonah

messages.subject: problems with "data frames"
parts:
Hi, Jonah.  We can talk about it on Friday.  Short answer is that when working with data and fitting models it's a real pain in the ass to keep working with a data frame.  I actually don't like the whole "data frame" thing as it can act as a straitjacket, it's a Stata way of thinking.

Here's an example.  I start with this model (for simplicity I'm assuming we have a stan_logit() alias):

stan_logit(y ~ dist + arsenic)
or
stan_logit(y ~ dist + arsenic, data="wells")

Ok, fine so far.  Now I decide I want to code as dist/100:
dist100 <- dist/100
stan_logit(y ~ dist100 + arsenic)

That worked fine.  Now the alternative:
dist100 <- dist/100 INSIDE "wells"
stan_logit(y ~ dist100 + arsenic, data="wells")

So here's my question:  can I do this:
dist100 <- dist/100 INSIDE "wells"
in a reasonable way?

Right now I have to first pull dist out of wells, then compute dist100, then put it back into wells, something like this:
dist <- wells$dist
dist100 <- dist/100
APPEND wells with dist100
(I don't remember how to do that last command but I know it can be done in one line.)

Anyway, that's the point.  In the midst of running regressions I play with data, for example creating a new predictor:
x_avg <- (x1 + x2 + x3)/3
or whatever.
If I have to keep putting things into the data frame just to run my regressions, that's a pain in the ass.  It's _not_ just "a bit more typing," it's actual additional lines of code, it makes things harder to follow.

In Stata world, you have a big data matrix and then pull out columns of it.  I don't see this as being R world.

A

We've been (at least Ive been) a bit sloppy with terminology and I think that's leading to some misunderstanding. Some of it has to do with the global environment but some of it is still a problem with local environments too. 

The real issue is that R will look for variables in parent environments (and then keep looking if it doesn't find them).  Often the global environment is the only one but it can also include local environments that themselves are parents to other environments and this is often just as problematic. It's really useful for some things but anything that isn't taken directly from user specified input can lead to trouble when it needs to be used later. Any specification of data that isn't directly input by the user is messy even if the data exists in an intermediate environment between the modeling function and the global environment. So even behavior that is natural to R is actually problematic for development of modeling software  because the same problem can occur no matter if the sole parent environment is the global environment or if there are layers of environments in between.

Ultimately it's really just that it's much harder to make robust software when you have to deal with R's handling of environments (not just global) instead of relying on the user to just tell you exactly what to use. 

I definitely see why being stricter about this can be a pain from a user perspective, so hopefully we can find a good compromise.

y1 <- list(a = a1, b = b1);
y2 <- list(a = a2, b = b2);

fit1 <- stan("foo.stan", data=y1);
fit2 <- stan("foo.stan", data=y2);

fit2 <- stan("foo.stan", data = list(a = a2, b = b2));

a <- a1;
b <- b1;
fit1 <- stan("foo.stan")

# load a second global data set
a <- a2;
b <- b2;
fit2 <- stan("foo.stan");

saying that at the point you have the y1 and y2 in the

> On Feb 3, 2017, at 4:14 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> You keep talking about "global" things. R has local environments.

Yes it does. And there's a top-level one called the global environment
about which R's doc says:

The global environment .GlobalEnv, more often known as the user's workspace,
is the first item on the search path. It can also be accessed by globalenv().
On the search path, each item's enclosure is the next item.

If you give R a variable (*not* a variable name), then
it searches up the environment chain from the current local
environment up to the global environment until it finds a definition
or fails.

Previously, RStan only read out of the global environment.
I didn't realize it got fixed so it'd read locally. I just
verified that you're right that it looks in the global environment
with RStan 2.14.

But lm() does *not* read out of the local environment when the
formula's given as a string.

$ x <- rnorm(100)

$ y <- 10 * x + 100 + rnorm(100)

$ foo <- function(n) { x <- rnorm(n); y <- 50 * x - 200 + rnorm(100); lm("y ~ x"); }

$ foo(200)

Call:
lm(formula = "y ~ x")

Coefficients:
(Intercept) x

99.89 10.03

So you can see it's reading out of the global environment, not
the function's local environment. If I define the formula without
quotes, it reads out of the local environment:

> bar <- function(n) { x <- rnorm(n); y <- 50 * x - 200 + rnorm(100); lm(y ~ x); }
> bar(200)

Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Coefficients:
(Intercept) x

-200.0 49.9


No clue as to what's going on but this is why I'm talking about
local vs. global behavior and why Jonah says it's been such a pain
in the ass to mirror the behavior of lm() etc.

A language like C or C++ would let you read a global variable in a function,
but not if it's declared after the function. Everything has to
exist when a function's defined---that's static lexical scoping.
R uses dynamic lexical scoping, which is why it's so damn confusing.
It waits until run time, then sees if it can find a definition floating
around in the environment somewhere. It's also one of the reasons
it's so slow, but that's another issue.

The main reason static lexical scope is so desirable is that it
allows you to reason about what your program's going to do from
just looking at the program. With dynamic lexical scoping, you have
to wait until run time. At that point, someone could've accidentally
dropped in another definition of a variable between your global and
that function call, and that one would get picked up. This is why
we all think it's so dangerous as a general practice.

> For example, if you call Stan within a function, Stan will take the data from the local environment within the function call, not the global environment.
>
> Here's a simple example:
>
> foo <- function(){
> a <- 3
> print(a)
> }
>
> a <- 5
> foo()
>
> If you do the above, it will print 3, not 5.

Yes, I understand that. See above. You're passing
the a ***by value*** here, not by name. This is the
distinction we're trying to get through to you.
> P.S. stan() takes data in the form of a list. stan_glm() takes data in the form of a "data frame" (a matrix).

And apparently more general than a matrix. It has
types for columns and apparently doesn't have to be
rectangular, which was news to me.

- Bob

I think the point is that with pipes you don't need

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problems with "data frames"
parts:
> On Feb 3, 2017, at 7:36 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Yes, R has local and global environments. It was just that I had the impression that you thought I wanted everything to be global.

I want it to be passed by value from a local environment
as a function argument.

y = ...
stan(..., data=y)

You want it to be picked up non-locally from within
the function reaching back to the nested calling environment.

y = ...
stan(...)

Now you may think this isn't very different, but in the first
version, the function stan() receives the data y as an argument.
That is, it gets the value.

In the second version, what happens is that the function stan()
has to go back into the environment that called it and look
for the variable y. This is *completely* different.

The thing that can cause subtle bugs in a language that
dynamically scopes like R is that the path for searching
for a value *will* go all the way out to the global
environment. So if you're in some function body and forget
to define y, then Stan will keep looking further out.
But you don't know what that sequence of nested
environments are when you write the function---that's what
it means to be dynamic. So you might get things by mistake.

So the long story is that yes, you want to look in
the environment and that implicitly looks all the way up
to the global environment. I only want to look at an
argument. Only local scoping and no nasty run-time surprises.

- Bob

I'd love to hear any suggestions anyone has. I have
this problem when fitting models, too. I try to be
careful to give all of my models meaningful names then
stick to that, but they wind up being too similar to
one another or too long.

One way to tame some of this complexity is to create
intermediate objects (even lists), as in:

run1 <- list(fit = fit1, sim = sim1)

The big win is that you then pass run1 around instead
of (fit1, sim1) and there are fewer names to memorize.
You may not like that you have to use run1$fit, but you
could always run it in an environment defined by run1.
Jonah cleaned up a lot of my case study code that way.

I actually find that clearer if there's a declared
structure somewhere than having all the bits and pieces
flying around. The use is much more consistent in that
it enforces the right naming. You can't make the mistake
of having sim1, fit1, sims2, fit2 (see the problem?).

- Bob
